subject: Communication
title: Power Distance: Who Decides?
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Power Distance: Who Decides?.

hook.text: In Denmark, a junior employee emails the CEO directly. In Malaysia, that would be career suicide.

buildup.text: Power Distance measures how much a society accepts unequal distribution of power. High PD = hierarchy is natural.

discovery.text: High PD countries (Malaysia, Philippines, Mexico) expect deference. Low PD (Denmark, Sweden, Israel) challenge authority.

twist.text: Korean Air crashes in the 1990s were partly caused by high power distance — co-pilots wouldn't correct senior pilots' errors.

climax.text: Power distance shapes everything: management style, classroom dynamics, parent-child relationships, and political systems.

punchline.text: Some cultures ask 'who decides?' Others ask 'why should anyone decide for me?'

quiz.question: What does high power distance in a culture indicate?

details.summary: Power distance measures how much a society accepts unequal distribution of authority. High power distance cultures like Malaysia and India expect hierarchy and deference. Low power distance cultures like Denmark and Israel encourage challenging authority and flat structures.
details.whyItMatters: Power distance shapes who speaks in meetings, how decisions are made, and whether subordinates will challenge a flawed plan. Misjudging it causes serious workplace failures.
takeaways: High power distance expects hierarchy and deference to authority
Low power distance encourages challenging senior figures
It directly affects decision-making and meeting dynamics

faq.question: How does power distance affect business meetings?
faq.answer: In high power distance cultures, the most senior person speaks first and decides. Subordinates rarely disagree publicly. In low power distance cultures, junior members are expected to contribute ideas. Running a flat-style meeting in a hierarchical culture silences people.

faq.question: Is high power distance always negative?
faq.answer: No. High power distance provides clarity, rapid decision-making, and social stability. Low power distance enables innovation and employee engagement. Each has advantages. Problems arise not from the level itself but from mismatches between expectations.
